We consequently introduced the compound concept for long-term modulation stating that the diffusion coefficients $\propto [B_0/B(t)]^n$, with $n = \alpha_t/\alpha_0$, and where $\alpha_t$ is the time-varying HCS ‘tilt angle’, and $\alpha_0$ is a constant. It is known from previous simulations (e.g., Potgieter and le Roux, 1992) that $\alpha_t$ plays a dominant role through drifts around solar minimum modulation, and that this role gradually subsides to be replaced by PDBs as the dominating modulation process around solar maximum modulation (see review by Potgieter, 1995). This means that $n$ is small ($n \to 0$) for minimum modulation, but must then increase with increasing solar activity ($n = 2$ to $5$), depending on the energy. We established that with $\alpha_0 \approx 7^\circ-15^\circ$, the amplitude of the 11 year cycle for 1.2–2.5 GV protons, helium and electrons could be reproduced. When applied to simulating the electron to proton ratio along the *Ulysses* trajectory, it turned out to be remarkably successful as the comparison with data shows in Figure 5. ## 5. Conclusions Observations from the *Ulysses* mission have contributed significantly to our basic theoretical understanding of cosmic ray modulation in the inner heliosphere, and at high heliolatitudes during solar minimum conditions. *Ulysses* observations during the next solar minimum period ($A < 0$) are vital. They will not only tell us the difference between consecutive solar minima, which from a drift point of view is vastly different, but will also enhance our understanding of how a complete 22-year modulation comes about. Observations during the present solar maximum period <!-- page 10 -->
are crucially important for progress in the theoretical understanding and modeling of cosmic ray modulation during these special epochs. The basic transport processes are relatively well understood but we still do not fully understand the relative importance of the major mechanisms over complete 11-year and 22-year cycles. The spatial form and rigidity dependence of the elements of the diffusion tensor are still mainly unknown, but progress is being made in this field. Major advantages are being made with new generation self-consistent CR-HD and CR-MHD modeling. They face similar difficulties than the ‘standard’ modulation models, but the potential to solve them on a more fundamental basis seems better. The role of perpendicular diffusion has become more important in heliospheric modulation, especially the assumption of its enhancement in the polar direction, but it is at the same time somewhat controversial (Fisk and Jokipii, 1999), and in apparent competition with the effects of the newly proposed HMF of Fisk (1996). Only more and better observations will tell which approach works better. The overall role of drifts seems to have somewhat diminished, but it is still a mechanism crucially needed to explain several major modulation features. The role of drifts during high solar activity is not well understood so that observations for the next few years, especially of charge-sign dependence, are most essential, and hopefully very enlightening. Long-term modulation is obviously a complicated interplay of at least the four major modulation processes. Comprehensive modeling of time-dependent modulation indicates that the diffusion coefficients are time-dependent. No unique set of modulation parameters exists – they seem to differ from solar minimum to solar minimum. Comprehensive time-dependent modeling requires propagating diffusion barriers - (including MIRs and GMIRs) - during increased solar activity to simulate 11-year cycles; it is simply not possible with an increasing wavy HCS alone, and it is not possible with a steady global increase in the Sun's total field alone as suggested by Cane *et al.* (1999). Successful modeling of long-term modulation needs a compound description of PDBs and a time-varying HCS superimposed on the base-line modulation given by the four basic mechanisms. The compound concept, as discussed in this review, is reasonably successful in explaining complete 11-year and 22-year cycles.

However, to describe the intensity of protons in the minimum of solar activity in 2009 with such a model, the value of the model parameter k (which is, in fact, the ratio of the regular component of magnetic field to its turbulent component) must be increased three times as compared with its value in the minima of the 22nd and 23rd cycles (Krymsky et al., 2013). <sup>2</sup> Key Laboratory of Dark Matter and Space Astronomy, Purple Mountain Observatory, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Nanjing 210023, China (Dated: February 27, 2025) ## ABSTRACT The spectra of galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) contain crucial information about their origin and propagation through the interstellar medium. When GCRs reach Earth, they are significantly influenced by the solar wind and the heliospheric magnetic field, a phenomenon known as solar modulation. This effect introduces time-dependent variations in GCR fluxes. The AMS-02 experiment has released time-dependent flux data for protons, electrons, and positrons, revealing clear correlations with solar modulation. Studies suggest that cosmic rays with the same charge, such as protons and helium nuclei, exhibit similar/same solar modulation parameters. In this work, we derive the LIS for protons and positrons under the assumption of a common solar modulation potential, using data from Voyager 1 and a 7-year average from AMS-02. Similarly, the LIS for antiprotons and electrons is derived by assuming they are governed by a separate solar modulation potential. We demonstrate that the time-dependent fluxes of positrons and protons can be accurately modeled using the same set of solar modulation parameters within a modified force-field approximation framework. Based on this, we predict the time-dependent fluxes of antiprotons using the corresponding electron flux data. ## 1. INTRODUCTION Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) are charged, energetic particles originating from cosmic accelerators, such as supernova remnants, and propagate throughout the Milky Way (Moskalenko & Strong 1998). Upon entering the heliosphere, they are modulated by the outward-moving magnetized solar wind plasma (Potgieter 2013). It is important to study the solar modulation as it is crucial for understanding the nature of GCRs, including their origins (Blasi 2013) and propagation mechanisms (Strong et al. 2007) within the galaxy. Additionally, solar modulation plays a critical role in the search for dark matter, as it affects low-energy antiproton and antideuteron fluxes (Lavalle & Salati 2012; Yuan & Bi 2015; Cui et al. 2017; Zhu et al. 2022). The propagation of GCRs within the heliosphere is described by Parker's transport equation (TPE) (Parker 1965). This equation can be solved using various methods, including numerical and analytical approaches. Usually, the force field approximation (FFA) (Gleeson & Axford 1967, 1968) is used to solve the equation as it is simple and enough to explain the observations. The recent experimental results have achieved significant breakthroughs that are instrumental in understanding the solar modulation effect as well as the GCRs physics, particularly those from Voyager, AMS-02, PAMELA and DAMPE (Stone et al. 2013; Adriani et al. 2011; Aguilar et al. 2017; Ambrosi et al. 2017). To date, only Voyager-1 and Voyager-2 have crossed the heliospheric boundary (Stone et al. 2013; Stone et al. 2019), providing direct measurements of the LIS in the energy range of a few to hundreds of MeV/nucleon. The AMS-02 collaboration has further contributed by publishing high-precision cosmic ray spectra (Aguilar et al. 2021a) and the evolution of some cosmic ray fluxes over time (Aguilar et al. 2018a,b), providing new opportunities to study the solar modulation for cosmic rays (CRs). The FFA cannot explain the fluxes itself as well as the changing over a long period of time with homogeneous parameters (Shen et al. 2021; Long & Wu 2024). Several methods have been proposed to modify zhucr@anhu.edu.cn duankk@pmo.ac.cn arXiv:2501.12625v2 [astro-ph.HE] 26 Feb 2025 <!-- page 2 -->
the FFA to account for the cosmic rays fluxes (Corti et al. 2016; Yuan et al. 2017; Zhu et al. 2021; Shen et al. 2021; Cholis & McKinnon 2022; Long & Wu 2024). Recently, AMS-02 released time-dependent flux data for protons (positrons, and electrons) spanning from 2011 to 2020 (to 2022) (Aguilar et al. 2021b, 2023a,b), offering new avenues to study solar modulation. In this study, we utilize two modified force-field approximation models to investigate the solar modulation of protons, positrons, and electrons. Both models successfully fit the daily and monthly fluxes of protons and positrons using the same set of parameters. Building on this, we predict the daily fluxes of antiprotons based on the corresponding electron fluxes data. ## 2. METHODOLOGY ### 2.1. *Solar Modulation* The existence of heliospheric magnetic field carried by solar winds causes the modulation of GCRs as they enter the heliosphere, resulting in suppressed fluxes of CRs. This phenomenon is known as solar modulation, and its effects are more pronounced at particle energies below 30 GeV/n (Potgieter 2013). The basic transport equation was first derived by Parker (Parker 1965). 3D time-dependent self-consistent modelling is a full solution to the CRs transport problem in the heliosphere, however it is a complicated task and requires a very large amount of computation. The FFA is a simplified method to solve this problem. Usually, the FFA requires the quasi-steady changes, spherical symmetry, etc, which are apparently invalid for short time scales. In fact, they are not fully valid even for the regular condition (Caballero-Lopez & Moraal 2004). However, the force-field formalism was found to provide a very useful and comfortable mathematical parametrization of the GCR spectrum even during a major Forbush decrease, irrespective of the (in)validity of physical assumptions behind the force-field model. So one can still benefit from the simple parametrization offered by the FFA for practical uses other than studying the physics of solar modulation, even if the FFA is not a physically motivated solution to the solar modulation problem at daily time scales (Usoskin et al. 2015). In this model, the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) flux is related to the local interstellar spectrum (LIS) flux as follows: $$
J^{\text{TOA}}(E) = J^{\text{LIS}}(E + \Phi) \times \frac{E(E + 2m_p)}{(E + \Phi)(E + \Phi + 2m_p)}, \quad (1)
$$ where $E$ is the kinetic energy per nucleon, $\Phi = \phi \cdot Z/A$ with $\phi$ representing the solar modulation potential, $Z$ and $A$ are the atomic number and mass number of the cosmic ray particle, respectively, $m_p = 0.938$ GeV is the proton mass, and $J$ denotes the differential flux of GCRs. The sole parameter in the FFA is the modulation potential $\phi$. ### 2.2. *Modified Force-Field Approximation* The force-field model assumes a quasi-steady-state solution to Parker's transport equation. However, observational GCR fluxes exhibit 11-year variations linked to solar activity. To account for this, a time-series of $\phi$ at different epochs is used to describe the data. Since a single parameter cannot adequately fit the monthly cosmic ray fluxes, a rigidity-dependent solar modulation potential is required (Siruk et al. 2024). In this study, we employ two modified force-field approximation models. First, we use Zhu's model from Zhu (2024), an extension of the standard force-field approximation. The solar modulation potential in this model is defined as: $$
\phi(R)_{\text{Zhu}} = \phi_l + \left( \frac{\phi_h - \phi_l}{1 + e^{(-R+R_b)}} \right), \quad (2)
$$ where $\phi_l$ and $\phi_h$ are the modulation potentials for low and high energies, respectively, $R$ is the rigidity, $R_b$ is the break rigidity and $e$ is the natural constant. A sigmoid function is employed to ensure a smooth transition between $\phi_l$ and $\phi_h$, which is necessary to model the gradual change in modulation potential across different energy ranges. The parameters $\phi_l$, $\phi_h$, and $R_b$ are free and determined through fitting. Second, we adopt Long's model from Kuhlen & Mertsch (2019); Long & Wu (2024), which introduces a power-law dependence on rigidity to account for variations in solar modulation. The solar modulation potential in this model is expressed as: $$
\phi(R)_{\text{Long}} = \phi_0 + \phi_1 \ln(R/R_0), \quad (3)
$$ with $$
J^{\text{TOA}}(E) = J^{\text{LISA}}(E + \Phi) \times \frac{E(E + 2m_p)}{(E + \Phi)(E + \Phi + 2m_p)} \exp\left(-g \frac{10R^2}{1 + 10R^2} \phi\right). \quad (4)
$$ where $\phi_0$, $\phi_1$, and $g$ are free parameters to be fitted. The parameter $g$ controls the rigidity dependence, allowing the model to capture the energy-dependent modulation effects more accurately. <!-- page 3 -->
2.3. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) We fit the two solar modulation $\phi(R)$ with three free parameters. The $\chi^2$ statistics is defined as $$
\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{[J(E_i; \phi(R)) - J_i(E_i)]^2}{\sigma_i^2}, \qquad (5)
$$ where $J(E_i; \phi(R))$ is the expected modulated flux, $J_i(E_i)$ is the measured flux, and $\sigma_i$ is the measurement error for the $i$-th data bin, with $E_i$ representing the geometric mean of the bin edges. The errors $\sigma_i$ include both statistical and systematic uncertainties, ensuring a robust fit. To minimize the $\chi^2$ function, we employ the MCMC algorithm within a Bayesian framework. In Figure 5 shows the two-dimensional fit of theoretically motivated solar halo models, based on a choice of different modulation potentials for positrons and electrons. Our best-fit model prefers a modulation potential of 475 MV for electrons, with no modulation (0 MV) of positrons. However, we note that the uncertainty on the positron modulation is quite large, due to the much smaller flux of the positron component. Calculating a one-dimensional uncertainty band for both electrons and positrons by minimizing over the other modulation potential provides a $5\sigma$ uncertainty range of $474_{-59}^{+55}$ MV for electrons and $0^{+223}$ MV for positrons, where we do not let the modulation potential to fall below 0. We note that our observation that the positron modulation potential is much smaller than the electron modulation potential closely matches theoretical expectations for the positively charged Solar Cycle 24, and also matched observations of charge sign-dependent solar modulation of electrons and positrons near Earth [52]. However, the quantitative value of the positron modulation potential in our analysis is likely unphysical due to systematic effects. Notably, because the $\gamma$-ray data cannot distinguish between ICS emission produced by an electron or positron, our fits only differentiate the components based on their input LIS spectra. The fact that positrons are highly sub-dominant (by a factor of $\sim$10-20) means that small errors in the electron LIS spectrum or modulation model will have outsized effects on positron modulation. Thus, while it is important to include contributions from both components, we only consider the electron modulation potentials to be well-modeled in our study, while, we consider the positron modulation value to primarily be a nuisance parameter that instead absorbs errors in our model. Examining our results, and in particular the halo spectrum shown in Figure 3, there is an indication of small (but only marginally statistically significant) anomalies that are worthy of comment. The first is at high energies, where we see a number of points that significantly exceed the predicted $\gamma$-ray flux. This includes a 30 GeV bump very close to the Sun, which is (on first inspection) interesting in light of the 30–50 GeV spectral dip observed from the solar disk in Ref. [27]. However, it would be difficult to correlate these two observations into a single coherent explanation, as the *Fermi-LAT* angular resolution at these energies is $\sim$0.1–0.2°, which is far smaller than the scale of the ICS emission, and the emission processes between the disk and halo differ. We note that there are also high-energy “excesses” in other spatial bins, but note that there is significant point-to-point variation in the spectrum in this region. In summary, we do not believe that either of features — although they may at first appear interesting — are indications of any significant deviations from the theoretically predicted solar halo model. The second spectral feature is more subtle, but critical for interpreting solar modulation models. We note that for low-energy data, higher solar modulation potentials ($\Phi_0 \sim 500$ MV) provide a better fit near the Sun ($\theta \lesssim 15^\circ$). This change is statistically significant, due to the fact that the error bars in this region are small. We note that the standard 500 MV model is not a good fit to the data in the closest regions ($<2.5^\circ$) from the Sun. However, we note that this region encodes both the energy range and angular area where uncertainties in the Fermi-LAT exposure (which is changing rapidly at low-energies), and the point-spread function (which is largest at low energy) are worst. Similarly, we note that lower solar modulation potentials provide better fits farther from the Sun, which despite the lower statistical significance may be more important due to the lower smaller errors. It is important to note, that the total log-likelihood fit in our models is dominated by the high photon counts of relatively low-energy $\gamma$-rays. This tension motivates us to examine alterations to the standard force-field potential model (Model I) in the next section. V. A CLOSER LOOK AT SOLAR MODULATION The key science result of our paper is that the first-order properties of the solar halo are well fit by simple force-field solar modulation models within a $\gamma$-ray energy range spanning 31 MeV–100 GeV, and from the position of the Sun out to an angular distance of $45^\circ$. Moreover, we note that the best-fit modulation potential for electrons calculated at 1 AU in ICS Model I ($\sim$475 MV) is consistent with the average modulation values calculated from fits to the local $e^+e^-$ data ($\sim$500 MV). However, our work in the previous section unveiled some regimes in which this simple model may not fit the $\gamma$-ray data. Thus, in this section, we closely probe alternatives to the simple force-field halo model (Model I). <!-- page 11 -->

Changes in Modulation Potentials Near the Sun We note that the best-fit modulation potential for electrons calculated for the ICS halo using Model I (~475 MV) is very consistent with the average modulation values calculated from fits to the local $e^+e^-$ data (typically ~500 MV). However, we note that these values need not be identical. First, the solar halo extends all the way to the Sun, measuring solar modulation in a regime that no cosmic-ray studies have probed. Second, the solar halo data probes the spherically symmetric modulation potential, which may differ significantly from the modulation potential in the ecliptic plane. This leads us to consider a simple conceptual model of solar modulation that is split into two different regimes. The dominant effect of solar modulation takes place between the heliopause and the Earth, which lies outside our $\gamma$-ray ROI. In this regime, changing the modulation potential between 0 MV and 1000 MV decreases the overall normalization and hardens the spectrum of the solar halo, but does not significantly affect the $\gamma$-ray morphology determined by Fermi-LAT data. The second regime corresponds to the subsequent solar modulation that occurs between the Earth and the Sun, and which lies inside our ROI. A key impetus for this paper is that solar modulation in this region has not been probed by cosmic-ray studies and is accessible only to our $\gamma$-ray observations. Modulation in this region controls the radial shape of the solar halo within our ROI, and also produces energy-dependent effects. However, the effect on the total normalization is smaller, as the majority of the modulation effect occurs between the edge of the heliosphere and 1 AU. Importantly, we note that the 45° edge of our ROI corresponds to electrons that have an average distance near 1 AU$^5$ from the Sun, mean- ing that the transition between these two regions occurs very close to the Earth’s position. Interestingly, previous work in Ref. [41] used Parker Solar Probe data to study modulation between the Earth and Sun, finding weaker modulation within 1 AU compared to expectations from the force-field model. Motivated by their work, we consider an alternative model where there is no additional modulation between the Earth and Sun, leading to a total modulation potential given by Eq. (4) in Model II. In Fig. 6 we calculate the heatmap for the electron and positron modulation potentials in this model, finding the best-fit modulation potential for electrons increases to a value of $576_{-56}^{+84}$ while the positron modulation potential remains consistent with $0_{-153}^{+153}$. This is consistent with the assumption that removing the additional effect of modulation near the Sun requires a larger modulation potential in regions outside 1 AU.

# THE MODULATION OF GALACTIC COSMIC RAYS IN THE HELIOSPHERE: THEORY AND MODELS M. S. POTGIETER Space Research Unit, Department of Physics, Potchefstroom University for CHE,
2520 Potchefstroom, South Africa **Abstract.** Almost all theoretical and numerical models for the modulation of cosmic ray in the heliosphere are based on Parker's transport equation which contains all the important basic physical processes. The relative importance of the various mechanisms is however not established and may vary significantly over 22 years. The simultaneous measurements of solar wind parameters, heliospheric magnetic field properties and cosmic rays over a wide range of energies and positions in the heliosphere have brought the re alization that modulation is much more complicated than what the original drift models predicted. In the process the sophistication of models based on solving Parker's equation has increased by orders of magnitude. A short review of the global modulation of cosmic rays is given from a theoretical and modelling point of view. **Key words:** Cosmic rays, modulation, heliosphere, solar activity ## 1. Introduction The long-term modulation of galactic cosmic rays (CRs) has been recorded by neutron monitors for almost two 22-year cycles. This record of high energy CRs shows clearly that the CR intensity-time profiles were peaked in the minimum modulation periods of 1965 and 1987 but plateau-like during the 1970's. The present minimum period, although only half way, seems to have similar features than the 1970's (McDonald *et al.*, 1996). One is inclined therefore to conclude that CRs are modulated according a simple 22-year variation in which global drift may be the dominating mechanism in general. This global behaviour was indeed predicted by numerical steady-state drift models developed in the early 1980's (Jokipii and Thomas, 1981; Kóta and Jokipii, 1983; Potgieter and Moraal, 1985). Our understanding of modulation for the decade since 1980 was strongly influenced by these predictions because they were clear and straight-forward. However, by the late 1980's it had become progressively evident that the large effects predicted by drift dominated models were not observed but that all of them, however, seemed to occur to some extent. For recent years, an important aspect of theoretical and modelling studies has been to establish and understand the relative roles of the major modulation mechanisms over a complete 22 year cycle. Apart from neutron monitor observations at Earth, a unique network of interplanetary spacecraft (*Pioneer 10 & 11, Voyager 1 & 2* and *IMP*) at various positions in the heliosphere has begun, since the late 1970's, to contribute significantly to our understanding of modulation. Since the launch of *Ulysses* in 1990, the global modulation picture has changed significantly. The simultaneous measurements of <!-- page 2 -->
solar wind parameters, heliospheric magnetic field (HMF) properties and CRs over a wide range of energies and positions brought the realization that the modulation of CRs is much more complicated than what 'standard' steady-state drift models predicted. In the process, the sophistication of the numerical models based on solving Parker's transport equation has increased by orders of magnitude. Because of numerous free parameters in these models, detailed and comprehensive predictions have however been difficult. The Pioneer/Voyager and Ulysses missions are therefore very important, not only for understanding the global aspects of modulation but also for limiting the number of free parameters in these numerical models. A short review is given of what we presently know about the global modulation of galactic CRs in the heliosphere from a modelling point of view. The role of CIRs and the acceleration and modulation of the anomalous component are discussed separately by Kóta and Jokipii (1998) and Jokipii and Giacalone (1998) respectively. For a list of review papers, see Potgieter (1995; 1997). ## 2. Cosmic Ray Modulation in the Heliosphere ### 2.1. THE TRANSPORT EQUATION AND DIFFUSION TENSOR The modulation of CRs is described by Parker's (1965) transport equation for the omnidirectional distribution function $f(\mathbf{r}, p, t)$ (related to the differential intensity by $j_T \propto p^2 f$) of CRs with momentum $p$, at position $\mathbf{r}$, and time $t$: $$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{K}^{(s)} \cdot \nabla f) - \mathbf{v}_d \cdot \nabla f - \mathbf{V} \cdot \nabla f + \frac{1}{3} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{V} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \ln p} + Q(\mathbf{r}, p, t). \quad (1)
$$ The diffusion tensor is: $$
\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} \kappa_{\parallel} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \kappa_{\perp \theta} & \kappa_A \\ 0 & -\kappa_A & \kappa_{\perp r} \end{bmatrix}. \quad (2)
$$ $\mathbf{K}^{(s)}$ is the symmetric part of the diffusion tensor with elements $\kappa_{\parallel}$ and $\kappa_{\perp}$, respectively the diffusion coefficients parallel and perpendicular to the mean background HMF, $\kappa_A$ is the 'drift' coefficient and $\mathbf{V}$ is the solar wind velocity. The first term on the right-hand side of equation (1) describes diffusion, the second term describes drift, with $\mathbf{v}_d$ the drift velocity, the third term describes the outward convection due to the solar wind, the fourth term the adiabatic energy changes and the fifth term, $Q(\mathbf{r}, p, t)$, a particle source e.g., for the anomalous component. The use of a steady-state with $\partial f / \partial t = 0$, and $Q(\mathbf{r}, p, t) = 0$, to model CR modulation during solar minimum conditions is justified and widely used. These terms cannot be neglected, however, when the role of time-dependent phenomena and termination shock acceleration are modelled. For clarity on the role of the diffusion coefficients consider a distribution function $f(r, \theta, p, t)$, with the respective function variables being radial distance, polar <!-- page 3 -->
angle, rigidity and time, and the two-dimensional transport equation in spherical polar co-ordinates: $$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{r^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left( r^2 \kappa_{rr} \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} \right) + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left( \frac{1}{r} \sin \theta \kappa_{\theta\theta} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} \right) + [-V - \langle v_d \rangle_r] \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} + \left[ -\frac{1}{r} \langle v_d \rangle_{\theta} \right] \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} + \frac{1}{3r^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} (r^2 V) p \frac{\partial f}{\partial p} + Q \quad (3)
$$ with $$
\langle v_d \rangle_r = - \frac{\operatorname{sign}(Bq)}{r \sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} (\sin \theta \kappa_{\theta r}) \quad \text{and} \quad \langle v_d \rangle_{\theta} = - \frac{\operatorname{sign}(Bq)}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} (r \kappa_{r \theta}). $$ The charge state of particles is given by $q$, the HMF by $B$, $\kappa_{r\theta} = \kappa_A \sin \psi$ and $\kappa_{\theta r} = -\kappa_A \sin \psi$, where $\psi$ is the HMF spiral angle. With $\kappa_{rr} = \kappa_{\parallel} \cos^2 \psi + \kappa_{\perp r} \sin^2 \psi$, it follows that the effective radial diffusion is dominated in the polar regions and inner heliosphere by the first term, and in the outer equatorial regions by the second term. Perpendicular diffusion in the polar direction is given by $\kappa_{\theta\theta} = \kappa_{\perp\theta}$. If perpendicular diffusion is assumed to be isotropic, then $\kappa_{\perp r} = \kappa_{\perp\theta}$. (See also Jokipii *et al.*, 1995a,b). From these expressions it follows that incorporating drift will lead to significantly different drift velocity fields depending on the sign of the polarity of the HMF and therefore to different density gradients for positively and negatively charged particles depending how dominant drift are made. Most importantly, if the density gradients are small, drift effects on modulation will also be small even if the drift velocities are quite large. Large values for $\kappa_{\parallel}$, and especially for $\kappa_{\perp}$, will therefore automatically reduce drift effects even if $\kappa_A$ is kept unchanged. Potgieter *et al.* (1989) and Potgieter and Burger (1990) illustrated that reducing drift effects is inevitable when 'standard' drift models were compared to observations e.g., proton radial gradients and electron modulation. Webber *et al.* (1990) showed that relatively large drift effects seemed required when models were compared to neutron monitor data, but that significantly reduced drift was required at energies $< 1$ GV. Several publication on altering drift and the other diffusion coefficients have since been published, demonstrating that our lack of knowledge of the diffusion tensor in the heliosphere is a severe handicap in understanding the detail of CR modulation. A few examples are given here. Burger (1990) discussed the effects of scattering and the random walk of field lines on drift and found that in principle drift can be influenced by all fluctuations with scales equal to or greater than the resonant wavelength. Jokipii (1993) illustrated that a finite scattering rate could significantly change drift trajectories in the heliosphere. Bieber *et al.* (1995) and Hattingh *et al.* (1995) studied the implications of diffusion coefficients derived from quasi-linear theory and a hard-sphere scattering model and concluded that a better understanding of the nature of turbulence throughout the heliosphere and its effect on perpendicular transport, in particular, is needed (Bieber and Matthaeus, 1997). The variable Sun controls the structure of the heliosphere and the modulation of cosmic rays through the level of solar activity, the tilt of the heliospheric current sheet, the velocity of the solar wind and the strength and turbulence of the interplanetary magnetic field (McDonald, Webber, and Reames, 2010). Determination of diffusion effects is a challenging astrophysical problem, because it requires an understanding of the properties of magnetic fields and turbulence, it also demands accurate theories for determining diffusion tensor (e.g. Pei et al., 2012). The inverse correlation between CRI and interplanetary magnetic field [$B$] has been known for a long time (e.g. Burlaga and Ness, 1998; Cane et al., 1999). Parallel diffusion coefficient [$K$] as well as the perpendicular diffusion coefficient [$K$] is assumed to be generally inversely proportional to $B$ in theoretical modeling of solar modulation (Jokipii and Davila, 1981; Reinecke, Moraal, and McDonald, 2000). Drift velocities of CRI increase with decreasing $B$. Thus, it would be interesting to look whether the $K$ and/or $K$ relation with $B$ shows any polarity-dependent effect, at least during low solar-activity periods, in view of our results showing the polarity-dependent CRI-response to changes in $B$. During $A<0$ periods (e.g. $\approx$1960 - 1970 and $\approx$1980 - 1990), when the solar field polarity is reversed, cosmic rays approach the sun from the equatorial region along the HCS. Analyses such as ours, involving various solar/heliospheric parameters in different polarity epochs and solar-activity conditions, are expected to improve our understanding of the unexplained aspects of solar modulation of galactic cosmic rays. ## 3. Conclusions We find that the CRI decreases at a faster rate with an increase in both SSN and $\Lambda$ as well as with $V$ and $B$ and their derivatives [$BV, BV^2$] when the solar magnetic parameter $A$ is negative than when $A$ is positive. Thus not only SSN and $\Lambda$ but also the parameters $V$ and $B$ exhibit different effectiveness in modulating the CRI during $A<0$ as compared to $A>0$ solar-polarity epochs. This rate is found to be faster by a factor of 1.5 to 2 in $A<0$ than in $A>0$, during the increasing and decreasing phases of solar activity cycles and even two to three times faster in low activity periods. More specifically, we find that during $A<0$ increasing phase of solar cycles, CRI decreases at about twice the faster rates with an increase in SSN, $\Lambda$, *B*, and *E* while this rate is about 1.5 times higher with *V*, $\sigma_B$, and $BV^2$, as compared to rates during a similar phase of other solar cycles in $A>0$ epochs. There is essentially no consistent difference in CRI effectiveness to changes in various parameters during high solar activity in different solar cycles. All four terms (convection, diffusion, drift, and adiabatic energy change) in Parker's transport equation involve *V* and/or *B* in one form or the other. Out of these four terms, only the curvature and gradient drifts are considered to be solar-polarity dependent.

The heliosphere has two distinct boundaries, namely the solar wind termination shock at an estimated $\approx 90$ AU, and the heliosheath beyond that. The current non-shock model can not distinguish between these boundaries, but this is not important in the current context. [10] The name “force field” originates from the fact that (8) can be written in the form $$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial r} + \frac{VP}{3\kappa} \frac{\partial f}{\partial p} = 0, \quad (9)
$$ where we have changed the variable from momentum, $p$, to rigidity, $P$. Particle rigidity has the dimensions of potential and the coefficient of the second term has the dimensions of potential per unit length, or a field - hence the name “force field.” [11] The rigidity $P_b = P_b(r, P)$ is obtained by integrating the characteristic equation from the initial phase space point $(r, P)$ to the point $(r_b, P_b)$ at the outer boundary $r_b$. If the diffusion coefficient is separable in the form $$
\kappa(r, P) = \beta\kappa_1(r)\kappa_2(P), \quad (10)

\int_{P}^{P_b(r,P)} \frac{\beta(P')\kappa_2(P')}{P'} dP' = \int_{r}^{r_b} \frac{V(r')}{3\kappa_1(r')} dr' \equiv \phi(r), \quad (11)
$$ where $\phi$ is called the force field parameter. When $\kappa_2 \propto P$ and $\beta \approx 1$ the solution reduces to the widely used form $$
P_b - P = \phi, \quad (12)
$$ so that the force field parameter becomes a rigidity loss or, alternatively, an energy or a momentum loss. Since it has the dimensions of potential, it is often called the force field potential. Typical values of $\phi$ vary from 300 to 1000 MV, from solar minimum to solar maximum conditions. It is often forgotten that the force field rigidity (or momentum) loss in the form (12) applies only to the special case of relativistic particles, $\beta = 1$, and the rigidity dependence $\kappa \propto P$. In all other cases $P_b - P = f(\phi, P)$. A case that is often studied with the force field approach is the modulation of low energy electrons in the range 1 to 100 MeV. These <!-- page 3 -->

This is due to the interpretation of the coefficient $VP/3\kappa$ as a field in (9). There is no physical reason why this field, force, or energy loss, is related to the true adiabatic loss. The force field energy loss originates from the introduction of the Compton-Getting spectral term $C$ in (8). It seems fortuitous that this energy loss is a reasonable approximation of the adiabatic energy loss in certain circumstances. Gleeson and Urch [1971] showed, in fact, that the force field energy loss in the form (12) is an upper limit of the true, adiabatic loss. # Sensitivity of cosmic ray modulation to the correlation length S. Parhi, J. W. Bieber, and W. H. Matthaeus Bartol Research Institute, University of Delaware, Newark, USA R. A. Burger School of Physics, Potchefstroom University for CHE, Potchefstroom, South Africa Received 6 August 2001; revised 1 February 2002; accepted 1 February 2002; published 30 April 2002. [1] Recent efforts to improve and complete modulation theory are described, emphasizing factors that arise in attempts to understand the diffusion tensor based upon turbulence theory and the theory of charged particle scattering. Direct numerical solutions of the transport equations are used to study sensitivity of cosmic ray modulation to the correlation length. It is shown that modulation is strongly influenced by the radial variation of the correlation length. This variation is still poorly understood, in part owing to the uncertain impact of pickup ion driven turbulence in the outer heliosphere and to practical difficulties in measuring the parallel correlation length in the outer heliosphere. INDEX TERMS: 2104 Interplanetary Physics: Cosmic rays; 2159 Interplanetary Physics: Plasma waves and turbulence; 2114 Interplanetary Physics: Energetic particles, heliospheric (7514) ## 1. Introduction [2] Solar modulation of cosmic rays is the process by which the Sun alters and regulates the intensity of galactic cosmic rays entering the heliosphere. Although an inverse relationship between solar activity and cosmic ray intensity has been recognized for 50 years [Forbush, 1954], the physical mechanisms underlying modulation remain poorly understood and continue to be an active area of research. [3] Aside from its intrinsic interest as a fundamental process in astrophysical plasmas, modulation plays an important role in other areas. For instance, consideration of modulation effects played a major role in recent pioneering observations of cosmic antiprotons [Asaoka et al., 2001]. Other examples are the new ideas about the large-scale [Fisk, 1996] and random [Jokipii, 2001] features of the interplanetary magnetic field that emerged from Ulysses observations of cosmic rays at high heliographic latitudes. [4] Central to quantitative models of solar modulation is the diffusion tensor which describes particle scattering by turbulence as well as gradient and curvature drifts. While the diffusion tensor and its spatial variation have traditionally been treated as free parameters that are adjusted to fit observations, recent efforts have explored a new approach in which the diffusion tensor is specified ab initio by particle transport theory, and its spatial variation is determined by turbulence transport models [Zank et al., 1996, 1998; Burger and Hattingh, 1998; Smith et al., 2001]. [5] This work focuses on one of the key parameters of ab initio theories: the correlation length of the magnetic turbulence. This quantity strongly influences diffusion coefficients for transport parallel and perpendicular to the large-scale field, but its variation with heliocentric distance ($r$) is very poorly understood. Turbulence transport theory suggests the correlation length may decrease with radius approximately as $r^{-0.3}$ owing to pickup ion-driven turbulence in the outer heliosphere [Zank et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2001], while direct measurement indicates the radial correlation length increases approximately as $r^{+1}$ [Smith et al., 2001]. Neither of these results is decisive, however. The theoretical formulations (especially of pickup ion effects) are likely incomplete, while the measurements describe the “wrong” correlation length. (Transport theory requires knowledge of the correlation of fluctuations parallel to the large-scale field, but measurements in the outer heliosphere yield a correlation length almost perpendicular to the field. ) This work employs numerical simulations to show that this uncertainty about the magnetic correlation length has major implications for ab initio modulation models. ## 2. Modulation Model [6] The modulation of galactic cosmic rays is described by Parker's equation [Parker, 1965]. In our model we describe the radial diffusion coefficient by $\kappa_{rr} = \kappa_{\parallel} \cos^2 \psi + \kappa_{\perp}^{r\phi} \sin^2 \psi$. Here $\kappa_{\parallel}$ is the diffusion coefficient parallel to the mean magnetic field, $\kappa_{\perp}^{r\phi}$ the diffusion coefficient perpendicular to the field in the radial/azimuthal direction and $\psi$ the spiral angle. We adopt a standard Parker model of the large-scale field, in which the mean field has no $\theta$ component. Hence $\kappa_{\theta\theta}$, the diffusion coefficient in the polar direction, is purely perpendicular to the mean field and is assumed to be larger than $\kappa_{\perp}^{r\phi}$ by a constant factor [Jokipii and Kota, 1989]. We use a steady state two-dimensional model that simulates the effect of a wavy current sheet [Burger and Hattingh, 1995] by using an averaged drift field with only an $r$ and $\theta$ component. We consider $\kappa_{\perp}^{r\phi}$ [Bieber and Matthaeus, 1997 (“BAM” for brevity)] as follows: $$
\kappa_{\perp}^{r\phi} = \frac{VR_L}{3} \left( \frac{\Omega_\tau}{1 + \Omega^2 \tau^2} \right), \quad (1)
$$ where $\Omega_\tau = 2R_L/3D_\perp$. Here $2D_\perp = D_{slab} + (D_{slab}^2 + 4D_{2D})^{1/2}$, $D_{slab} = \delta B_{slab}^2 l_{slab}/2B^2$, $D_{2D} = \delta B_{2D} l/B$, where $l_{slab}$ is the correlation length for slab-component fluctuations, $\delta B_{slab}^2$ is the variance of slab geometry fluctuations, $\delta B_{2D}^2$ is the variance of two-dimensional fluctuations [Matthaeus et al., 1990] and $\tilde{l}$ is the turbulence ultrascale [Matthaeus et al., 1995, 1998]. $R_L$ is the particle Larmor radius, $V$ is the particle speed, and $\Omega = V/R_L$ is the angular gyrofrequency. The timescale $\tau$ describes the decorrelation of the particle trajectories in the turbulent field. Throughout this paper we take the ultrascale to be a fixed multiple of the correlation length, $\tilde{l} = 200l_{slab}$. The parallel diffusion coefficient is given by $\kappa_{\parallel} = \lambda_{\parallel}V/3$, with the mean free path $\lambda_{\parallel}$ defined as in Zank et al. [1998] equation (4). We employ a slab spectrum model with Kolmogoroff ($k^{-5/3}$) inertial range, and a flat ($k^0$) energy range for wavenumber $k \lesssim 1/l_{slab}$. [7] The heliospheric boundary is assumed to be at 100 AU. The solar wind speed is 400 km/sec in the equatorial plane and increases to 800 km/sec in the polar regions. The tilt angle $\alpha$ of the wavy current sheet is set at 20°, a value appropriate for low solar activity. The interstellar proton spectrum as a function of rigidity is as given in Burger et al. [2000]. Note that the radial dependence of $\delta B^2$ follows from the models of Zank et al. [1996]. <!-- page 2 -->

It is remarkable that allowing these two free parameters to vary per time interval we can fit the time-dependent AMS-02 electron and positron fluxes rather accurately. Introducing in addition a linear model relating these two parameters to solar wind parameters, we can reproduce not only the AMS-02 measurements, but also the PAMELA electrons fluxes which do not overlap with the AMS-02 electron fluxes. We can also predict the electron and positron fluxes beyond the range for which data has been published. We stress that our method is significantly faster than numerical methods and more accurate than the standard force field model. It can thus be applied to large datasets with fine time binning like the current AMS-02 data. An important issue in modulation modeling therefore concerns the spatial dependence of these coefficients where the situation is still unsatisfactory, especially concerning the latitude dependence of these coefficients. Until about 1990, the general practice was to assume $K_{\parallel, \perp} \propto 1/B_p$, where $B_p$ is the Parker geometry for the HMF. In the majority of modeling studies $B_p$ has been replaced by $B_m$ the modified HMF as given above. It is interesting to note that in earlier studies, the modulation group in Potchefstroom (see *Potgieter and Moraal* [1985]; *Potgieter and Burger* [1990]) successfully used $K_{\parallel} \propto (1+r^2)$, which is independent of latitude which qualitatively seems to be required by recent Ulysses magnetic field observations (e.g., *Balogh et al.*, [1995]). Recently, *Haasbroek and Potgieter* [1995] illustrated that in order to obtain qualitative agreement with Ulysses high latitude proton observations, one probably has to assume $K_{\parallel} \propto (1+r)$, which on its part is compatible to what $1/B_m$ gives at high latitudes. For the purpose of this study the assumption of $K_{\parallel, \perp} \propto 1/B_m$ was maintained. This has also the practical advantage that the small radial gradients predicted by drift models for the $A > 0$ magnetic epoch (e.g., ~1970 to ~1980; ~1990 to present), as emphasized by *Potgieter* [1985] and *Potgieter et al.* [1989], are improved to become more compatible with observations. Whether this modification alone is adequate to fit the observed radial and latitudinal gradients for protons and other nuclei in the inner and outer heliosphere at all latitudes simultaneously [*Haasbroek and Potgieter*, 1995; *Reinecke et al.*, 1995], is still uncertain and needs further investigation. A second step was to make assumptions for the rigidity dependence of $K_{\parallel}$ and $K_{\perp}$. In this regard, the predictions at 1 AU for $K_{\parallel}$ by *Bieber et al.* [1994] and the results of *Müller-Mellin and Wibberenz* [1995] are most useful and will be studied as a primary object of this paper. A general form used for $K_{\parallel}$ in modeling studies is $$ K_{\parallel} = K_0 \beta \frac{K_R}{R_0} \frac{B_0}{B_m} \quad (5) $$ Here $\beta$ is the ratio of the speed of the cosmic ray particles to the speed of light, $K_R$ gives the rigidity dependence in GV, with $R_0 = 1.0$ GV, $B_0$ is the value of the HMF at Earth and $K_0$ is a constant which determines the value of $K_{\parallel}$ in units of $1.0 \times 10^{22} \text{ cm}^2 \text{ s}^{-1}$. The corresponding parallel mean free path at Earth, with $c$ the speed of light in cm s$^{-1}$, is given by $$ \lambda_{\parallel} = \frac{3K_{\parallel}}{c\beta} = \frac{3K_0 K_R}{c R_0} \quad (6) $$ *Bieber et al.* [1994] discussed three different models for calculating the parallel mean free path: (1) The damping model - slab geometry (DMSG - approach). (2) The damping model - composite slab - two-dimensional geometry (DMCSG - approach) and (3) the random sweeping model - slab geometry (RSMSG - approach). The different values for $\lambda_{\parallel}$ calculated from the three approaches, together with that of *Müller-Mellin and Wibberenz* [1995] and predicted for QLT are reproduced and shown in Figure 1. The corresponding $K_0$ values as used in equation (5) are given in Table 1. It follows from Figure 1 that approaches 1, 3, and 5 give $\lambda_{\parallel}$ similar above 0.1 GV but differ significantly below that, whereas approaches 2 and 4 give about the same values below 1 GeV but differ at higher rigidities. The last two cases also give significantly higher values than approaches 1, 3, and 5 over the entire rigidity range presented in Figure 1, except below 0.01 GV for approach 1. In the next section the effects of these different values for $\lambda_{\parallel}$ and especially the different rigidity dependencies on modulation will be illustrated. An issue that needs special attention is the question how to handle $\lambda_{\perp}$. *Bieber et al.* [1994] clearly illustrated the difficulties involved in deriving $\lambda_{\parallel}$, let alone $\lambda_{\perp}$. It is important to realize that in an axially symmetric model, based on equation (1), perpendicular diffusion can contribute to modulation in two ways. First, in calculating the effective radial diffusion coefficient $K_{rr} = K_{\parallel} \cos^2\psi + (K_{\perp})_{rr} \sin^2\psi$, and second the contribution through $K_{\theta\theta}$ in equation (4). The general importance of the latter has recently been reemphasized by *Jokipii et al.* [1995a, b]. In particular, *Kóta and Jokipii* [1995a] pointed out that large - scale transverse magnetic fluctuations as observed by Ulysses [*Smith et al.*, 1995] would reduce cosmic ray access over the solar poles. Important is that the mentioned fluctuations together with the random walk of fields lines may cause diffusion in the polar direction to vary differently from the other direction normal to the background magnetic field. *Kóta and Jokipii* [1995a] argued that diffusion could be much more rapid in the polar direction than in the radial direction to the extent that $K_{\pi} \approx (K_{\perp})_{\pi} \propto 1/r$ and $K_{\theta\theta} \approx (K_{\perp})_{\theta\theta} \propto r$, when $r \gg 1$ AU. Unfortunately, it is not known from theory what its spatial and rigidity dependence may be. In order to avoid another totally free parameter, it was assumed for this study that both $(K_{\perp})_{\pi}$ and $(K_{\perp})_{\theta\theta}$ have the same rigidity and spatial dependence as $K_{\parallel}$. Concerning its value, observations of Jovian electrons with Ulysses [*Ferrando et al.*, 1993] seem not to support a $K_{\theta\theta} ( > K_{\pi})$ as large as *Jokipii et al.* [1995a, b] argued. It was therefore assumed for the majority of solutions that $(K_{\perp})_{\pi} = (K_{\perp})_{\theta\theta} = aK_{\parallel}$, with $a = 0.01$ or $0.02$, which seems in reasonable agreement with observations on Jovian electrons [*Ferrando et al.*, 1993]. The exception was when perpendicular diffusion was enhanced in the polar direction through simply increasing $(K_{\perp})_{\theta\theta}$ in order to illustrate its effect on electron modulation. Whether $a = 0.02$ is large enough to account for the small latitudinal effects observed by Ulysses will be reported elsewhere [*Hattingh et al.*, 1997, *Potgieter et al.*, 1997]. Gradient, curvature, and neutral sheet drifts were handled numerically according to the well-known approach of *Potgieter and Moraal* [1985] for two-dimensional models. (For a review of these models, see *Burger and Hattingh* [1995]). Recent modelling with a three-dimensional steady-state model *Hattingh et al.* [1997] confirmed that the results of the two-dimensional model are qualitatively in agreement with that of the two-dimensional model. In contrast to $K_{\parallel}$ and $K_{\perp}$, theory gives a straight forward expression for $K_A$ under the assumption of weak-scattering: $$ K_A = (K_0)_A \frac{\beta R}{3B}, \qquad (7) $$ which is also dimensionally correct with the constant $(K_0)_A$ dimensionless. With $(K_0)_A = 1.0$; 0.5, and 0.2 respectively, this equation describes what *Potgieter et al.* [1989] called "full $\equiv 100\%$" "half $\equiv 50\%$" and "20%" drifts. When $B = B_p$, $(K_0)_A = 1.0$ and the "tilt angle" $\alpha = 0^\circ$, the most ideal drift situation possible is described.

In Fig. 1, we compare the contribution from the adiabatic term, $\partial/\partial p (p^3\mathbf{V} \cdot \nabla f) / (3p^2)$ to the advective term, $\nabla \cdot (C\mathbf{V}f)$. Comparison with other secondary-to-primary ratios The prediction for the $ ar{p}/p$ ratio is calculated. The default $ ar{p}$ production cross-sections embedded in GALPROP [8, 54, 55] is used here. As shown in FIG. 4, compared with the conventional DR model suggested in [10], which adopted a force-field approximation, the DRC-CM model (see Table I) yields 30%~60% higher $ ar{p}$ production around a few GeV. It seems that an inclusion of a convection mechanism and incorporating a charge-dependent heliospheric modulation model both influence substantially to the $ ar{p}/p$ ratio. The DRC-CM model agrees fairly well with the PAMELA data below 1 GeV and above 10 GeV. At moderate energies, the DRC-CM model yields a slightly lower $ ar{p}/p$ ratio. CONCLUSION For the first time, we use the PAMELA measurements of hydrogen and helium isotopes to perform an elaborate study and a comparison on cosmic ray propagation models. Accurate and reliable constraints are generated by using the $^2$H/$^4$He and $^3$He/$^4$He ratios combined with the $Z \le 2$ primaries. Several hints can be inferred from our results. First, a global fit on both the modulate and unmodulated data disfavors the widely used force-field approximation. Instead, the tension between CR propagation models and the observations can be released by incorporating the time-, charge-, rigidity-dependent CM solar modulation model. Second, various models are comprehensively studied and compared by using statistical methods. From a quick $\chi^2$ minimization analysis, it is found that only models including the reacceleration effect can accommodate individual ratios and fluxes. A Bayesian analysis provides evidences which strongly support the DRC-CM model over the DR-CM model. The $ ar{p}/p$ ratio not involved in the fitting procedure further demonstrates the plausibility of our DRC-CM model and the robustness of the estimated diffusion spectral index $\delta$. At least, the DRC-CM model show good agreements with all the $Z \le 2$ data. Third, the value of $\delta$ is determined to be close to 1/3, which indicates a Kolmogorov-type turbulence. This estimated $\delta$ based on $Z \le 2$ data is slightly smaller than that value derived from the B/C ratio. However, systematics uncertainties may contribute to this discrepancy, which will be further investigated in the future.

MODELING To put our observations into the context of conventional modulation analysis, we have examined the predictions of a simple force field model. In particular, we examine whether the linear character of the plots in Figures 9 and 10 is consistent with such a model. The force field model of solar modulation of GCRs is a well known spherically symmetric model of solar wind convection, adiabatic deceleration, and diffusion. The combined effect of these processes is expressed by a single “modulation parameter” that depends only on position (radius) and time. The force field approximation results from a differential equation for the evolution of the phase space distribution function $f$ of cosmic rays as a function of radius and momentum $p$, where the rigidity spectrum $j(P)$ is related to $f(p)$ by $j(P) \propto P^2 f(p)$. Our modeling approach is based on that of Caballero-Lopez & Moraal (2004). The force field model itself (Gleeson & Axford 1968) comes from simplifications of the equation to a form that can be solved by the method of characteristics, so that the solution $f(r, p)$ is constant along contours of the characteristic equation. This relates the spectrum at a position within the heliosphere to the spectrum at a different momentum on the outer boundary; this is the LIS. With some further assumptions the characteristics reduce to the form $P_b - P = \phi$, where $\phi$ is the time-dependent “force field parameter” or “modulation parameter” that expresses a decrease in rigidity from the outer boundary to the location of interest, which is a reasonable approximation **Figure 11.** Like Figure 9, for calculations using a force field model as described in the text. Each line is a linear fit to model results for a 1 GV bin in apparent cutoff rigidity, ranging from the 0–1 GV bin at the top to the 15–16 GV bin at the bottom. to the adiabatic deceleration in some circumstances (Caballero-Lopez & Moraal 2004). While the distribution function $f$ is constant along characteristics, the expression for the rigidity spectrum $j$ has the additional factor of $P_b^2/P^2$ reflecting the difference in the magnitude of the momentum at the two places, so that $$ j(P) = \frac{P_b^2}{P^2} j_b(P_b), \quad P_b(P, t) = P + \varphi(t). \quad (10) $$ We use yield functions for protons and alpha particles from Clem & Dorman (2000) that are parameterized, along with several other potentially interesting functions, in Table 1 of Caballero-Lopez & Moraal (2012), though we use a different definition of DRF. MODELING APPROACH Once inside the heliosphere GCRs are subjected to an outward convection by the solar wind, adiabatic deceleration due to the expanding solar wind, diffusion along and across the turbulent HMF, and gradient, curvature and HCS drifts in the global HMF. These processes are responsible for altering the differential intensities of GCRs as a function of energy (rigidity), position in the heliosphere and time (solar activity). We simulate the transport of GCRs within the heliosphere by including all of these modulation processes into a full three-dimensional (3D) numerical model to compute the differential intensity of GCRs at different radial distances from the Earth up to the HP and spectra at the Earth over the rigidity range 10 MV - 70 GV. The VLIS's are specified as an initial condition (unmodulated spectra) at the HP. The predicted small modulation beyond the HP, as simulated by e.g., Scherer et al. (2011); Luo et al. (2015), is neglected. ## 4.1. Modulation model The model is based on the numerical solution of Parker's transport equation (Parker 1965) which follows the basic transport equation (TPE) for charged particle motion in large and small scale fluctuating magnetic fields, and averaged over the pitch and phase angles of propagation particles, with the assumption that GCRs are approximately isotropic. For the heliosphere this TPE is described as: $$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = -\vec{V}_{sw} \cdot \nabla f - \langle \vec{v}_D \rangle \cdot \nabla f + \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{K}_s \cdot \nabla f) + \frac{1}{3} (\nabla \cdot \vec{V}_{sw}) \frac{\partial f}{\partial \ln p} \quad (1)
$$ where $f(\vec{r}, p, t)$ is the omnidirectional GCR distribution function, $p$ is momentum, $t$ is time, and $\vec{r}$ is the vector position in 3D. If $P$ is particle rigidity, the differential intensity is given by $P^2f(p^2f)$. The first two terms shown on the right-hand side of this equation represent outward convection caused by the expanding solar wind with velocity ($\vec{V}_{sw}$) and the averaged particle drift velocity $\langle \vec{v}_D \rangle$ (pitch angle averaged guiding center drift velocity) i.e. particle drift caused by the HMF's gradients, curvatures and the wavy HCS. The third term represents spatial diffusion described by the symmetry diffusion tensor $\mathbf{K}_s$. When the TPE is written in heliocentric spherical coordinate system, the three coordinates $r, \theta$, and $\phi$ represent radial distance, polar and azimuth angles, respectively. According to this system, the Earth is located at 1 au in the equatorial plane with $\theta = 90^\circ$. In order to solve the TPE, six elements in this tensor related to diffusion are to be specified: $K_{rr}$, $K_{r\phi}$, $K_{\theta\theta}$, $K_{\phi r}$, and $K_{\phi\phi}$. These five diffusion coefficients in terms of diffusion parallel and perpendicular to the HMF direction are as follows: $$
K_{rr} = K_{\parallel}\cos^2\psi + K_{\perp r}\sin^2\psi. \quad (2)
$$ $$
K_{\theta\theta} = K_{\perp\theta}. \quad (3)
$$ $$
K_{\phi\phi} = K_{\perp r}\cos^2\psi + K_{\parallel}\sin^2\psi. \quad (4)
$$ $$
K_{\phi r} = (K_{\perp r} - K_{\parallel})\cos\psi\sin\psi = K_{r\phi}. \quad (5)
$$ This means, for example, that the effective radial diffusion coefficient $K_{rr}$ is a combination of the parallel diffusion coefficient ($K_{\parallel}$) and the radial perpendicular diffusion coefficient ($K_{\perp r}$), with $\psi$ the spiral angle of the background HMF; $K_{\theta\theta} = K_{\perp\theta}$ is the effective perpendicular diffusion coefficient in the polar direction; $K_{\phi\phi}$ describes the effective diffusion in the azimuth direction and $K_{\phi r}$ diffusion in the $\phi r$-plane. The fourth term in the right hand side of Equation 1 represents adiabatic energy changes which depends on the sign of the divergence of $\vec{V}_{sw}$. If $\nabla \cdot \vec{V}_{sw} > 0$, adiabatic energy loss occurs as is the case in most of the heliosphere, <!-- page 5 -->
except perhaps inside the heliosheath where we assume that $\nabla \cdot \vec{V}_{sw} = 0$; see also Langner et al. (2006). Adiabatic energy changes becomes dominant at lower rigidity in the case of modulated spectra for protons, antiprotons and GCR isotopes; see illustrations of this process by Moraal & Potgieter (1982); Strauss et al. (2011). The drift velocity can be written as follows: $$
\langle \vec{v}_D \rangle = \nabla \times K_D \frac{\vec{B}}{B}, \qquad (6)
$$ where $K_D$ is the generalized drift coefficient, and $\vec{B}$ is the HMF vector with magnitude $B$. When Equation 1 is rewritten not showing the drift velocity explicitly, then a generalized propagation tensor replaces the diffusion tensor and four elements must then be added to describe gradient and curvature drift: $K_{r\theta}$, $K_{\theta r}$, $K_{\theta\phi}$, and $K_{\phi\theta}$. The three components of the drift velocity (in the radial, polar and azimuth directions) in terms of these elements of the propagation tensor are then given by: $$
\langle \vec{v}_D \rangle_r = -\frac{A}{r \sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} (\sin \theta K_{\theta r}), \quad \langle \vec{v}_D \rangle_{\theta} = -\frac{A}{r} \left[ \frac{1}{\sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi} (K_{\phi\theta}) + \frac{\partial}{\partial r} (r K_{r\theta}) \right], \quad \langle \vec{v}_D \rangle_{\phi} = -\frac{A}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} (K_{\theta\phi}), \qquad (7)
$$

Modulation must be regarded as a complicated balance of diffusion, drifts, convection, and adiabatic cooling, none of which can be neglected. Crudely, one may view the effect of drifts as introducing an additional convection velocity which adds vectorially to the wind velocity. It is clear that the resultant “effective” convection velocity can differ substantially from the solar-wind velocity. However, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the gradient and curvature drifts have zero divergence and do not contribute to the adiabatic cooling. Nor can the drift by itself produce modulation if the wind velocity is identically zero. Unfortunately, because the drift velocities are not simple functions of heliocentric coordinates, it is difficult to find analytic solutions which give quantitative insight into the effect of the large drift velocities for cosmic rays in the solar wind. In order to illustrate some of the effects of drifts, we examine two simplified examples. Consider first a one-dimensional wind which flows in the positive $x$ direction with constant velocity $V_w$, and, furthermore, let nonrelativistic ($\alpha = 2$) or relativistic ($\alpha = 1$) particles propagate with diffusion coefficient $\kappa$ and drift velocity $V_D \hat{e}_x$. We require that at the outer boundary $x = D$, $U(x = D, T) = AT^{-[y+(\alpha-1)/2]}$, and at the inner boundary, $x = 0$, we impose the reflecting boundary condition given in equation (9). It is clear that the shape of the energy spectrum remains a power law with index $-\gamma$, so we suppress the energy dependence and simply require $U(X = D) = 1$. The solution for the density (or intensity) $U(x)$ can be written, setting $(2+\alpha\gamma)/3 = \eta$, $$
U(X) = \left\{ \frac{1 + v_D/v_w}{\eta} - 1 + \exp[(v_w + v_D)x/\kappa] \right\} / \left\{ \frac{1 + v_D/v_w}{\eta} - 1 + \exp[(V_w + v_D)D/\kappa] \right\}, \quad (10)
$$ and the logarithmic gradient becomes $$
G = \frac{1}{U} \frac{dU}{dx} = \frac{v_w}{\kappa} \left\{ \left( 1 + \frac{v_D}{v_w} \right) \exp \left[ (v_w + v_D)x/\kappa \right] \right\} / \left\{ \frac{(1 + v_D/v_w)}{\eta} - 1 + \exp \left[ (v_w + v_D)x/\kappa \right] \right\}. \quad (11)
$$ These functions are plotted in Figures 5 and 6 for various values of $v_D/v_w$ for $V_w D/\kappa = 3$ to illustrate the effects of the drifts. Notice that setting $V_w = 0$ in equations (10) and (11) yields $U(x) = 1$ and $G = 0$, a necessary consequence of the fact that the drift by itself produces no modulation. Despite this, however, in the presence of solar-wind-induced particle gradients, the drifts can substantially alter the overall modulation—either increasing it or decreasing it— as is shown dramatically in Figures 4 and 5. Depending on the sign of $A$, this drift velocity has a $y$-velocity toward (or away) from the plane $y = 0$, with the $x$-velocity peaked in the $y = 0$ plane and being outward (or inward). The differential equation for the cosmic-ray density $U(x, y)$ becomes $$
\frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial y^2} - \frac{(V_w + v_{Dx})}{\kappa} \frac{\partial U}{\partial x} - \frac{v_{Dy}}{\kappa} \frac{\partial U}{\partial y} = 0. \quad (13)
$$ This equation was solved numerically for $|y| < D_1$ and $-D_2 \le x \le 0$, subject to the boundary condition $U(x = 0, y) = 1$ (outer boundary). At $x = -D$, $y$ we imposed a zero-flux boundary condition $\partial U / \partial x - V_w U = 0$ (corresponding, for example, to $(2 + \alpha\gamma)/3 = 1$ in eq. [9]). We assumed $l_y \ll D$, so that at $y = \pm D$, the drift is in the $y$-direction and we expect that $U(x, y)$ approaches $\exp(V_w x / \kappa)$. Before solving numerically, we cast equation (13) into dimensionless form by defining the variables $$
\begin{aligned} x_1 &= x \frac{V_w}{\kappa}, \\ y_1 &= y \frac{V_w}{\kappa}, \end{aligned} \quad (14)
$$ in which case equation (13) can be written $$
\frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial x_1^2} + \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial y_1^2} - \left(1 + \frac{v_{Dx}}{V_w}\right) \frac{\partial U}{\partial x_1} - \frac{v_{Dy}}{V_w} \frac{\partial U}{\partial y_1} = 0.
$$ This equation was solved using a relaxation technique for the parameters $V_w D / \kappa = 3$, $V_w l_x / \kappa = 1$, $V_w l_y / \kappa = 0.3$, $A = \pm 10$. It was found that a mesh spacing of 0.075 in $V_w x / \kappa$ gave sufficient accuracy. The results for the density $U(x_1, y_1)$ and logarithmic gradient $G = U^{-1} \partial U / \partial x_1$ for $A = -10$ are displayed in Figures 7 and 8 and for $A = +10$ in Figures 9 and 10. The errors due to the finite mesh size are expected to be of the order of 10% or less in the gradients. Since the solutions are symmetric in $y$, only positive $y$ is plotted. In each of the Figures (7-10) the modulation solution without drifts is shown by a dashed curve. Clearly the effect of the particle drifts on the total modulation is substantial. Several salient qualitative points emerge from the figures. First, notice that the effect of the drift is most pronounced near $y = 0$, which corresponds to the solar equatorial plane in this crude illustration. To some extent this behavior is an artifact resulting from the imposed requirement that the solution go to the zero-drift solution at large $y$. This requirement has no analog in the spherical solar wind. We will confine our attention only to the curves corresponding to small values of $y$. A particularly intriguing feature of the solutions is the reduction of the logarithmic radial gradient which occurs for both signatures of the magnetic field ($A$). This may have some bearing on the small magnitude of the cosmic-ray radial gradient measured by deep-space probes. Another particularly interesting result of the calculations is that the magnitude of the modulated particle intensity also depends on the sign of $A$. <!-- page 7 -->

CONCLUSIONS We have discussed the properties of charged-particle drifts in the solar-wind magnetic field and have pointed out that the drift velocities are large, and that they can make a significant contribution to the modulation of cosmic rays. The purpose of this paper is to indicate the general nature of the drift effects through the use of several illustrative and highly idealized calculations. We have refrained from making direct comparisons with the observed patterns of cosmic-ray modulation. Such comparisons require more realistic model calculations which retain the spherical geometry of the interplanetary medium. This will be the subject of future work. Particle drifts affect both the modulated intensity and the gradient of cosmic rays. The precise effect of the drift depends on the geometry of the magnetic field. The main implication of the present calculations is that drifts will have to be accounted for quantitatively in models of cosmic-ray modulation before comparisons with the observational data become meaningful.

Another indication of the role of gradient and curvature drifts came in the form of a 22-year variation in the direction of the daily anisotropy vector in the galactic CR intensity as measured by NMs from one polarity cycle to another (Levy, 1976; Potgieter and Moraal, 1985). Potgieter et al. (1980) also discovered a 22-year cycle in the differential response function of NMs used for geomagnetic latitude surveys at sea-level in 1965 and 1976 (see also Moraal et al., 1989). Some of the key outcomes of gradient, curvature and current sheet drifts as applied to the solar modulation of CRs, are: <!-- page 24 -->
1. Particles of opposite charge will experience solar modulation differently because they sample different regions of the heliosphere during the same polarity epoch before arriving at Earth or at another observation point. Particle drift effects inside the heliosheath, on the other hand, may be different from upstream (towards the Sun) of the TS. 2. A well-established 22-year cycle occurs in the solar modulation of galactic CRs, which is not evident in other standard proxies for solar activity (see Figure 6). This is also evident in the directional changes of the diurnal anisotropy vector with every HMF polarity reversal (e.g., Potgieter and Moraal, 1985; Nkosi et al., 2008; Ngobeni and Potgieter, 2010) and from the changes in differential response functions of NMs obtained during geomagnetic latitude surveys. 3. The wavy HCS plays a significant role in establishing the features of this 22-year cycle in the solar modulation of CRs. 4. Cosmic ray latitudinal and radial intensity gradients in the heliosphere are significantly different during the two HMF polarity cycles and repeated ideal modulation conditions will display a 22-year cycle (e.g., Heber and Potgieter, 2006, 2008; Potgieter et al., 2001; De Simone et al., 2011). An illustration is shown in Figure 9 of how the computed radial gradients change with kinetic energy for the two polarity cycles at different positions in the heliosphere. In Figure 10 the difference caused by drifts in the computed latitudinal proton gradients between the two polarity cycles is shown as a function of rigidity in comparison with the observed gradient from PAMELA and Ulysses for the period 2007 (De Simone et al., 2011). 5. Cosmic ray proton spectra are softer during $A > 0$ cycles so that below 500 MeV the $A > 0$ solar minima spectra are always higher than the corresponding $A < 0$ spectra (Beatty et al., 1985; Potgieter and Moraal, 1985). This means that the adiabatic energy losses that CRs experience in $A < 0$ cycles are somewhat different than during the $A > 0$ cycles (Strauss et al., 2011a,c). This also causes the proton spectra for two consecutive solar minima to cross at a few GeV (Reinecke and Potgieter, 1994). 6. Drift effects are not necessarily the same during every 11-year cycle, not even at solar minimum because the recent solar minimum was different than other $A < 0$ cycles. The intriguing interplay among the major modulation mechanisms changes with the solar cycles (Potgieter et al., 2013). 7. Drifts also influence the effectiveness by which galactic CRs are re-accelerated at the solar wind TS (e.g., Jokipii, 1986; Potgieter and Langner, 2004a). However, it is unclear whether particle drifts play a significant role in the heliosheath and to what extent drift patterns are different than in the inner heliosphere. Particle drifts, as a modulation process, has made a major impact on solar modulation theory and was eclipsed only in the early 2000s when major efforts were made to understand diffusion theory better together with the underlying heliospheric turbulence theory (as reviewed by Bieber, 2003 and McKibben, 2005). It was also then finally realized that particle drifts do not dominate solar modulation over a complete solar cycle but that it is part of an intriguing interplay among basically four mechanisms and that this play-off changes over the solar cycle and from one cycle to another. The latest prolonged solar minimum brought additional insight in how this interplay can change as the Sun keeps on surprising us (Potgieter et al., 2013). <!-- page 25 -->
